blocks.text: Say: “He is Allah, the One[1];

Allah, exalted is He, introduces Himself to us through His names and attributes in these few words. Out of His mercy to human beings, just as He has provided what their bodies need, He has sent down what gives life to their souls. He says: “Likewise, We have revealed to you a revelation by Our command.” [Ash-Shūrā 42:52]. One of the greatest ways revelation brings the human heart to life is by making its Creator known to it.

The surah begins with Allah’s command ﴿قُلْ﴾, “Say.” The Prophet ﷺ conveyed this ayah as he received it, including the command itself. Among the meanings the commentators have drawn from this is that every Muslim should learn this belief and teach it to others. A Muslim comes to know their Lord through revelation and conveys that knowledge with the clarity in which it came. Complicated language and excessive argument should never become barriers to understanding it.

The ayah comes in the form of an answer to a question. Asking about the Creator is among the questions that arise from human nature. Just as people want to know where they come from and how they came into this world, their innate disposition drives them to learn who created them. Consider Allah’s words “When My slaves ask you concerning Me, I am indeed near[83].” [Al-Baqarah 2:186]. He uses the conditional wording «وإذا سألك» as though it is in a servant’s nature to ask about their Lord. Al-Ikhlas makes the Creator known to the servant even when the servant has forgotten to ask.

Some have explained that ﴿هُوَ﴾ at the start of the ayah is a pronoun introducing an important statement. In Arabic, this construction prepares the listener to receive something weighty. Here that statement is ﴿اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ﴾, an affirmation that Allah is One. “Allah” is the proper name of our Lord, exalted is He. Some scholars distinguish al-Wāḥid and al-Aḥad by explaining that aḥadiyyah means Allah is unique in His very being and also in His attributes and acts. No one resembles Him in knowledge, power, or mercy, and no one can govern the affairs of creation as Allah, exalted is He, governs them.

When we consider the surah’s place near the end of the Mushaf, we find that we have already read many accounts of prophets and their peoples. In them we have seen the effects of Allah’s power, mercy, and kindness to His servants. He delivers people from destruction, aids the oppressed, destroys the oppressor, heals the sick, and guides those who have gone astray: “every day He is engaged in some matters[8].” [Ar-Raḥmān 55:29] It is as though the surah answers a question that arises in the believer’s heart after those ayahs and accounts. Who did all of that? ‘Say: “He is Allah, the One[1];’

It was Allah who saved Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when he was thrown into the fire. Ibrahim said, “Allah is Sufficient for us, and He is the best Protector[84].” [Al-Bukhari 4563], and Allah said, “O fire, be cool and safe for Abraham.” [Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:69]. It was Allah who turned the women’s scheme away from Yusuf, peace be upon him. Yusuf said, “Unless you protect me from their guile, I may succumb to them”, and Allah says, “So his Lord answered his prayer and protected him from their guile.” [Yūsuf 12:33–34]. It was Allah who saved Yunus, peace be upon him, when he called out in the darkness, “None has the right to be worshiped except You. Glory be to You! I have certainly done wrong”. Allah, exalted is He, says, “So We answered his prayer and rescued him from distress.” [Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:87–88].

He is the One who drowned Pharaoh, showed kindness to Yusuf in prison, and gave the believers victory at Badr despite their weakness, “Allah had helped you at Badr when you were weak” [Āl ʿImrān 3:123]. We see the oneness affirmed by this surah in the acts of Allah that the whole Quran tells us about. When believers long for such kindness, relief, and victory, they know whom to turn to. That is what the next ayah brings out, “Allah, the Eternal Refuge[2].”

The Prophet ﷺ said that Al-Ikhlas “is equivalent to a third of the Qur'an.” [Muslim 811]. Despite this great virtue, the surah is only four ayahs long. Think also of Ayat al-Kursi. The Prophet ﷺ asked Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, may Allah be pleased with him, which ayah in Allah’s Book was greatest. When he answered that it was Ayat al-Kursi, the Prophet ﷺ affirmed his answer and congratulated him on his knowledge [Muslim 810]. That ayah teaches us about Allah, His knowledge, His sustaining of all, and His dominion. Al-Fatihah, which the Prophet ﷺ told us is the greatest surah of the Quran, brings together praise of Allah and asking Him for guidance [Al-Bukhari 4474].

Those who reflect on the Quran should take care that the search for subtle meanings and less obvious insights does not distract them from the great truths the Quran came to plant in hearts, foremost among them Allah’s oneness. A person may memorize Al-Ikhlas in childhood and recite it every day, yet still need to reflect on its meanings and examine their own state in light of them. This is how its effect comes to be seen in their worship, their fear and hope, and their reliance on Allah.

When a group of jinn heard the Quran, among the first ways they expressed the effect of its guidance on them were these words, “that guides to the right way, so we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord.” [Al-Jinn 72:2]. Singling out Allah for worship was among the greatest truths they received from the Quran.

Allah has the right over His creation to be worshipped alone. The Prophet ﷺ explained to Muʿadh, may Allah be pleased with him, that Allah’s right over His servants is “that they should worship Him (Alone) and should not worship any besides Him.” [Al-Bukhari 2856]. A person can become occupied with the rights people owe one another and overlook the right of the One who created them all.

The Companions’ belief that Allah is One was more than a conviction in their hearts. Its effect could be seen in the stands they took and the things they did. As Bilal, may Allah be pleased with him, was tortured in Makkah, he kept repeating, “Ahad, Ahad (One, One)” [Ibn Majah 150]. Although the polytheists could hurt him, he held fast to his servitude to Allah and refused their demands that he abandon his religion. In accounts of the Prophet’s life, this same expression is mentioned as the Muslims’ rallying cry at Badr. Their belief remained firm through changing circumstances. When they were vulnerable, they did not abandon Allah’s oneness out of fear of the polytheists. In victory and strength, they held to the same belief they had stood by in hardship.

A person deals with other people and makes use of practical means all day, while their heart moves between fear, hope, love, and eagerness. They need to renew their awareness of Allah’s oneness continually, so their attachment to created beings does not grow so strong that they forget their Creator. For this reason the following declaration of Allah’s oneness is prescribed a hundred times a day, “None has the right to be worshipped but Allah, the Alone Who has no partners, to Him belongs Dominion and to Him belong all the Praises, and He has power over all things” [Al-Bukhari 3293].

The importance of these truths in the believer’s life is reflected in what the Prophet ﷺ did. In Witr he would recite Al-Aʿla, then Al-Kafirun, then Al-Ikhlas [Abu Dawud 1423]. In the two sunnah rakʿahs of Fajr he would recite Al-Kafirun and Al-Ikhlas [Muslim 726]. The two surahs complement one another. In Al-Kafirun the servant disavows the worship of anything besides Allah. In Al-Ikhlas the servant recalls Allah’s uniqueness in His being, attributes, and acts, and remembers that He alone deserves worship and is the One to turn to in need.

After a long day of dealing with people, seeking a livelihood, and attending to needs, believers end their day by reciting these surahs. In light of their meanings, they examine what they did during the day. Did they place their hope and trust in Allah, or did their hearts become too attached to the means they used? In making choices, did they put pleasing Allah ahead of pleasing people? Praying during the night helps them take stock of themselves and bring the meanings of Allah’s oneness to mind. Allah says, “Indeed, worship at night is more effective[3] and more conducive to proper recitation[4].” [Al-Muzzammil 73:6].

Then believers recite the two surahs again in the sunnah prayer of Fajr, beginning their day mindful of the belief that should govern their actions and relationships. Their circumstances may change between hardship and ease. The truth of Allah’s oneness with which they end one day and start the next remains the same. What they need is to reassess their deeds and the feelings of their hearts in its light.

quranNotes.text: [1] He is Alone, without a partner, indivisible and distinct from all else. The only true deity, unique in His essence, attributes, and actions.
[2] He is absolute, perfect, complete, self-sufficient; the one eternally and constantly required and sought; all existence depend upon Him; all matters ultimately return to Him.
[83] Allah’s nearness means that one does not need to raise his voice or to ask for intercession in order that his prayers be answered.

[84] This is one of the greatest Dhikr (remembrance) during times of hardship. Ibn ‘Abbās (رضي الله عنهما) reported: “Hasbunā Allāh wa ni‘ma al-Wakīl (Allah suffices us, He is the best of Protectors), was said by Abraham (عليه السلام) when he was thrown in the fire and was said by Muhammad (ﷺ) when it was said: “People have regrouped for you, so fear them”, their belief grew firmer and they said: “Allah suffices us, He is the best of Protectors”.” [Al-Bukhārī: 4563]
[8] Such as giving life and causing death, enriching some and impoverishing others, elevating some and debasing others, etc.
[3] Or "getting up at night is more difficult...," meaning that it can only be done by sincere believers.
[4] i.e., for reciting, hearing, and understanding of the Qur’an.
[26] It is reported in an authentic Hadīth that Abraham said, while being thrown into the fire, “Allah is sufficient for us and He is the best Protector.”
[39] The darkness of the night, the sea, and the whale's belly.
[38] The second was his companion, Abu Bakr.

blocks.text: Allah, the Eternal Refuge[2].

Once a servant knows that Allah is One and that no one resembles Him in His attributes or acts, they know whom to turn to in need. Then comes Allah’s statement, “Allah, the Eternal Refuge[2].” Allah is named explicitly again in this ayah. The ayah does not say “He is Aṣ-Ṣamad.” One lesson to reflect on is to repeat the name of one’s Lord, seeking blessing in His remembrance and bringing His greatness to mind.

Among the explanations the commentators give for Aṣ-Ṣamad is that He has no cavity and neither eats nor drinks. This makes clear His complete independence of His creation. Allah says, “Who feeds but is not fed” [Al-Anʿām 6:14]. A person needs food and drink. No sooner is one need met than another arises, while Allah, exalted is He, has need of no one.

It is also said that Aṣ-Ṣamad is the One whose attributes are perfect. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, is reported to have explained that He is the Master whose mastery is perfect, the Forbearing whose forbearance is perfect, the Self-Sufficient whose independence is perfect, the All-Knowing whose knowledge is perfect, and the All-Wise whose wisdom is perfect [Al-Bayhaqi, Al-Asmāʾ waṣ-Ṣifāt, 98]. Just as Allah is unique in His attributes, He has perfection in every one of them. He alone provides, and His generosity is perfect. He alone governs affairs, and His kindness and wisdom are perfect. His mercy is beyond anything any of His creatures can attain.

This clarifies the connection with the third meaning of Aṣ-Ṣamad, the Master to whom all creatures turn in their needs. When people face a difficulty, they look for someone capable of solving it and do their best to reach the person most able to help. How then can someone know that Allah is perfect in knowledge, power, mercy, and generosity, yet turn their heart away from Him toward someone who is themselves in need of Allah?

What Aṣ-Ṣamad means for a servant goes beyond asking their Lord aloud. It also concerns the love, need, and hope the servant carries in their heart. One view of the origin of the name “Allah” links it to al-walah, intense attachment and longing. The intensity of attachment can be illustrated by what happens when a young camel is weaned and separated from its mother. It longs for her intensely and continues to call out in a way that expresses its need for her and its wish to return to her. The example helps us grasp attachment and need and draws no comparison between the Creator and a created being. However many people a person loves, there are forms of love, submission, and need in the heart that belong to Allah alone, exalted is He. The servant cannot do without Him in any of their affairs.

We see this turning to Allah in the story of Musa’s mother, when He said to her, “when you fear for him, cast him into the river” [Al-Qaṣaṣ 28:7]. A mother usually draws her child close when she fears for him and tries to keep him away from danger. Allah commanded Musa’s mother to do something contrary to what mothers usually do in that situation. He said, “when you fear for him, cast him into the river, and do not fear or grieve. We will surely return him to you, and will make him one of the messengers.” [Al-Qaṣaṣ 28:7]. Musa was saved through his mother’s obedience to Allah’s command and trust in His promise, even though the water looked dangerous.

This trust in Allah grows from knowing His power and also from certainty in His justice, wisdom, and the truth of His promise. We see it in Hud’s stand, peace be upon him, when he faced his people alone and said, “So plot against me all together, then give me no respite.” Then he explained why his heart was at ease, “I put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no moving creature but He holds it by its forelock[27]. My Lord is on a straight path[28].” [Hūd 11:55–56]. He knew that all his people were under Allah’s authority and power, and that his Lord would neither wrong him nor break His promise.

One of Allah’s most beautiful names is Al-Muʾmin. One of its meanings is that He gives His creatures security from ever being wronged by Him. In turning to Allah to meet their needs, the servant turns to the One who has the power to meet them, secure in His perfect knowledge, wisdom, and justice. This is why affirming Allah’s oneness in worship is among the means by which believers attain security. Allah says, “Those who believe and do not mix their faith with falsehood[25] are the ones who will be secure, and it is they who are rightly guided.” [Al-Anʿām 6:82].

Just as the believer goes to Allah with their needs, they turn to His revelation to learn what pleases Him and what He has commanded. It is inconsistent to depend on Allah for what one wants and then dispense with His guidance when deciding how to live and act.

Turning to Allah still involves taking practical steps. Allah has ordered life around causes and means. Someone who wants fruit tills the ground, sows a seed, and waters and tends it. Allah has made cultivation the usual path to obtaining fruit. A person does not give up planting and ask Allah to send fruit down from the sky.

So too, people who fall ill look for treatment and make use of it. The Prophet ﷺ said, “There is no disease that Allah has created, except that He also has created its treatment.” [Al-Bukhari 5678]. They remember that healing is from Allah, as in the Prophet’s supplication, “heal the patient, for You are the Healer. No healing is of any avail but Yours” [Al-Bukhari 5743]. A person works to earn a livelihood knowing that Allah is the Provider. They take the steps that lead to victory while certain of Allah’s words, “victory only comes from Allah” [Al-Anfāl 8:10].

Allah has set human life on the use of practical means. Constantly dealing with them, however, can make someone so absorbed in them that they lose sight of the One who decreed them and controls their outcomes. Allah says of what is on earth, “We have made all that is on earth as an adornment for it” [Al-Kahf 18:7]. Part of the test posed by this adornment is that people become absorbed in the visible means before them and forget Allah’s ordering of them. Allah is “the First[2] and the Last[3]” [Al-Ḥadīd 57:3]. He determined the means before they existed, and affairs return to Him after people make use of them. No cause works independently of His power, and no result comes about except by His will.

People may use the means that have usually brought them to their goal and still fail to get what they hope for. Those means may even produce results contrary to what they expected. At such times the effect of faith in Allah as Aṣ-Ṣamad becomes evident. People who pin their hopes solely on the means may lose hope when they fail. If their hearts have been attached to Allah from the beginning, they still hope for His help and favor, even when the means they expected to benefit from are no longer available.

In the migration of the Prophet ﷺ, we see practical measures and complete reliance on Allah come together. He arranged the provisions and means of travel they would need and someone to guide them on the route [Al-Bukhari 3905]. When the polytheists reached the cave, Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said, “If any of them should look under his feet, he would see us.” In response, the Prophet ﷺ did not remind Abu Bakr of their precautions. He said, “O Abu Bakr! What do you think of two (persons) the third of whom is Allah?” [Al-Bukhari 3653]. The Quran also tells us that he said, “Do not grieve; Allah is with us.” [At-Tawbah 9:40]. His reliance on Allah was already there before he took those measures, while he took them, and when the danger intensified. It did not begin only after the measures could no longer protect him.

Allah brought about miracles at the hands of His messengers to show people that the familiar order of causes places no limit on His power, exalted is He. The staff of Musa, peace be upon him, became a snake and the sea parted for him. ʿIsa, peace be upon him, raised the dead with Allah’s permission.

Allah gave this community a special gift in the Quran. It brings together revelation to guide people and a miracle that demonstrates the truth of the message. A believer who is certain of the Quran’s truth does not need to witness such perceptible miracles for themselves in order to believe in Allah’s power. At the beginning of Al-Baqarah, Allah describes the people who receive guidance as “those who believe in the unseen” [Al-Baqarah 2:3]. The believer is certain that Allah governs affairs whether they follow the causes they are used to or run counter to them. They do not wait for the means to fail before recognizing their need for Allah and attaching their heart to Him.

The difference between being attached to Allah and being attached to what He gives becomes clear when worldly circumstances change. Allah says, “There are some people who worship Allah on the edge [of faith][6]: if something good comes to them, they are content” [Al-Ḥajj 22:11]. Such a person has made their peace of mind depend on some worldly good that comes to them. When their circumstances change, their faith is shaken. This world never remains in one state, as Allah says, “We alternate among people these days” [Āl ʿImrān 3:140]. The believer attaches their heart to their Lord who does not die, following Allah’s command, “Put your trust in the Ever-Living Who never dies” [Al-Furqān 25:58].

The believer recalls this meaning when saying in supplication, “I have sought shelter for my back with You” [Al-Bukhari 247, Iman Companion translation of the meaning], entrusting their affairs to Allah and asking Him for protection and safety. When they say after prayer, “O Allah! Thou art Peace, and peace comes from Thee” [Muslim 591], they remember that the well-being they hope for does not depend on improved circumstances alone. They seek it from their Lord.

Knowing Allah’s most beautiful names goes beyond memorizing their meanings. The servant comes to know their Lord better by reflecting on the effects of these names in the Quran and in their own life. When they read Yusuf’s story, peace be upon him, they can reflect on how Allah arranged his affairs through the hardships he went through, all the way to the point when Yusuf, peace be upon him, said, “My Lord is gracious to whom He wills.” [Yūsuf 12:100] Reflecting on this deepens their understanding of Allah’s name Al-Laṭīf. Similarly, when a person faces a need, turns to their Lord, and reflects on what Allah made easy for them, they understand more of His generosity and freedom from need.

Growing used to hearing these meanings can make the heart less responsive to them, as happens in other parts of life. A person may visit someone who is ill and feel their heart soften as they remember the gift of good health. After repeatedly seeing illness, they may feel less moved. They may long to visit the Sacred Mosque and weep at the first sight of it, then have to make a conscious effort in later visits so familiarity does not dull their sense of its greatness. Likewise, a person may often hear about Allah’s names and attributes and discuss their meanings. They still need to reflect on them anew and bring their effects to mind, so their sense of Allah’s greatness and their need for Him does not weaken.

A person may speak at length about Allah’s names and attributes and discuss their meanings often, while their share of humility and awareness of their need for Him grows small. This is why they need to return to the Quran and learn about their Lord in the way Allah chose. He knows best what sets their heart right, “Does He not know His Own creation[4], when He is the Most Subtle, the All-Aware?” [Al-Mulk 67:14]. Among the Prophet’s supplications is one that brings together calling on Allah by His names and seeking benefit from His words, “to make the Quran the springtime of my heart, the light of my chest, the clearing of my sorrow, and the removal of my worry” [Ahmad 3712].

Hearing reminders alone is insufficient to make these meanings take root in the heart. People become more attached to what they give their time and effort to. A person does not need to be reminded every morning of the importance of getting what they want in this world. How much they think about such things and how hard they work to obtain them make their hearts more attached to them. Likewise, love and reverence for Allah grow with the servant’s time and effort in obeying Him, keeping up prayer, remembrance, and supplication, and learning their religion and teaching it to others.

When someone wants to grow in sincerity toward Allah, they need to go beyond listening to reminders about sincerity or sharing them. They strive with themselves so what they learn influences their worship and conduct. Allah says, “How excellent is the reward of those who do [righteous] deeds!” [Āl ʿImrān 3:136]. One fruit of knowing that Allah is Aṣ-Ṣamad is that this knowledge shows in the servant’s life. They turn to Him in need, seek His help in their efforts, hope in Him in hardship and ease, and do not forget Him when practical means become available.

[27] i.e., Allah is in full control over all His creatures.

[6] i.e., with uncertainty, hypocrisy, or heedlessness.

blocks.text: He neither begets nor is He begotten,

In this ayah Allah denies having a child or a parent. ﴿لَمْ يَلِدْ﴾ denies that He has a child, and ﴿وَلَمْ يُولَدْ﴾ denies that His existence came from another. Allah, exalted is He, is unlike created beings, who are known by their lineages and come into being through one another.

It is reported that the polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ, “Name the lineage of your Lord for us.” The report relates that Al-Ikhlas was then revealed [At-Tirmidhi 3364]. Reports differ about who asked. It is said they were polytheists, and it is also said they were People of the Book. The question reveals an error in how they conceived of Allah. They wanted to know His lineage as they knew the lineages of created beings. The surah rejects that conception at its root.

This differs from asking about one’s Lord out of a desire to know and worship Him. People are concerned to know their origins and lineage. ʿAbdullah ibn Ḥudhāfah, may Allah be pleased with him, once asked the Prophet ﷺ, “Who is my father?” [Al-Bukhari 93]. We come to know Allah through what He tells us about Himself, without comparing Him to created beings or supposing that He has a lineage like theirs.

Attributing a child to Allah goes beyond making a false statement about Him. In a sacred Hadith, Allah explained that the child of Adam’s denial of the resurrection is a denial of what Allah says. Then He said, “As for his abusing Me, it is his saying that Allah has begotten children, while I am the One, the Self-Sufficient Master Whom all creatures need, I beget not, nor was I begotten, and there is none like unto Me.” [Al-Bukhari 4974].

The Quran makes clear how grave it is to attribute a child to Allah. Allah says, “at which the heavens are about to be torn apart, the earth split asunder, and the mountains tumble down.” “because they have ascribed to the Most Compassionate a son.” [Maryam 19:90–91]. If the heavens, earth, and mountains nearly tear apart from the gravity of these words, how could they seem slight to a believer who knows and reveres their Lord? Revering Allah means feeling how these words diminish what is due to Him, declaring Him far above such a claim, and never letting repeated exposure make it seem trivial.

One effect of believing in this ayah is that the servant turns directly to Allah. People who wish to reach a powerful person may need the help of one of his children or relatives to get their needs met. Allah, exalted is He, has no child or parent through whom the servant might draw near to Him or by whose help they might obtain what Allah does not approve of.

There is great mercy in this for Allah’s servants. Anyone who commits a sin known only to Allah need not expose what Allah has concealed by revealing it to someone else in order to be forgiven. They turn to their Lord in repentance and ask His forgiveness. Musa, peace be upon him, did this when he said, “My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me,” and the answer came directly, “Then He forgave him” [Al-Qaṣaṣ 28:16].

blocks.text: and there is none comparable to Him.”[3]

The surah closes by denying that anything resembles Allah, exalted is He. He has no counterpart or equal in His very being, His attributes, or His acts. This is among the meanings of His words, “Do you know anyone equal to Him?” [Maryam 19:65]. That is, do you know of anyone like Him or comparable to Him?

One of the fundamental errors in knowing Allah is judging His attributes by those of created beings. A person then assumes that what human beings are incapable of cannot be an attribute of Allah. The Quran corrects this conception in His words, “There is nothing like unto Him[8]” [Ash-Shūrā 42:11].

This error can take the form of assuming that whatever one can conceal from people is also hidden from Allah. He says, “Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal?” [Al-Baqarah 2:77]. It can also take the form of wanting to know Allah in the same way one sees and touches created beings. The Children of Israel said, “we will never believe you until we see Allah openly” [Al-Baqarah 2:55]. And when they saw people devoted to their idols, they said, “make for us a god just as they have gods.” [Al-Aʿrāf 7:138]. These situations differ, but they come from the same root, judging the Creator by created beings. The believer receives what Allah has told them about His names and attributes without likening Him to His creation or denying Him an attribute of perfection because created beings are incapable of it.

This ayah completes the meanings of the surah. Allah is One in His being, attributes, and acts. He is Aṣ-Ṣamad, the One to whom all creation turns in its needs. He has no child and no parent. The surah closes by denying that there is anyone like Him whom a person might turn to besides Him for what they seek from Him, or imagine to have the power to compel Allah to do what they want.

There is mercy for human beings in this. Allah illustrates the difference between the one who worships Him alone and the one who associates partners with Him in the example, “a slave owned by several quarrelsome masters, and a slave owned by only one master” [Az-Zumar 39:29]. The first belongs to quarreling partners. Each wants his own demands met. He can hardly please one of them before angering another. The second belongs to one man and knows whom he works for and whom to obey.

So it is with the heart. If it were attached to everyone from whom it hoped to benefit or whose harm it feared, and its servitude were divided among people and means, it would suffer from being pulled in different directions and trying to please everyone. Out of His mercy, Allah commanded people to worship Him alone, devoting their belief, worship, and love to Him and returning to His Book to learn what they should do.

One subtle point about the arrangement of the surahs at the close of the Mushaf is that, after introducing Himself to us in Al-Ikhlas, Allah teaches us how to seek refuge in Him in Al-Falaq and An-Nas, ‘Say, “I seek refuge with the Lord of the daybreak,’ [Al-Falaq 113:1] and ‘Say, “I seek refuge with the Lord of mankind,’ [An-Nās 114:1]. Whoever is certain that no one equals Allah in His ability to protect them and ward off harm turns to Him seeking refuge from the evils around them and the whisperings they experience within themselves.

Holding firmly to the Quran does not mean people will never suffer harm. Plots were made against the Prophet ﷺ, and it is established that he was affected by magic [Al-Bukhari 5765]. Allah says of those who grew intensely resentful when they heard the Quran, “The disbelievers would almost strike you down with their malicious gazes when they hear the Reminder” [Al-Qalam 68:51]. One fruit of holding firmly to the Quran, therefore, is to know whose help and protection to seek when facing harm.

The Prophet ﷺ said to ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmir, may Allah be pleased with him, regarding the two surahs of refuge, “use them when seeking refuge in Allah, for no one can use anything to compare with them for the purpose.” [Abu Dawud 1463]. Al-Falaq and An-Nas are among the greatest words with which a servant seeks refuge from evil. One way to benefit from them is to read them with the meanings of Al-Ikhlas in mind, certain of the power of the One in whom one seeks refuge and aware of how deeply one needs Him. Hence the saying, “A staff depends on the one who wields it, and Al-Fatihah on the one who recites it.” It points to the importance of the heart’s state and certainty when reciting ruqyah or seeking refuge. Whether and when the harm is lifted remain in Allah’s hands.

Among the meanings that strengthen a servant’s certainty when seeking refuge is that Allah chose for them to seek refuge in Him by the name ﴿رَبِّ الْفَلَقِ﴾, identifying Him as the Lord of daybreak. The One who takes away the darkness of night and brings the light of morning is able to take away the worry and grief that have befallen them. Just as the light of morning emerges gradually until the darkness lifts, relief can come little by little through Allah’s kindness and ordering of affairs. The servant should not be impatient for the harm to be lifted. They continue to seek refuge in Allah, at peace with His power and His wisdom in determining when relief will come.

quranNotes.text: [3] The Prophet (ﷺ) says that reading this surah (surat al-Ikhlās) equals reading one third of the Qur’an. [Al-Bukhāri and Muslim]
[8] In His essence, His attributes, or His deeds.

blocks.text: Out of His mercy to human beings, Allah provides food for the body and has given guidance for the heart and mind. He sent down revelation as spirit and light. Allah says, “Likewise, We have revealed to you a revelation by Our command.” [Ash-Shūrā 42:52]. The heart needs its nourishment as much as the body does. The body hungers for food. When the heart forgets its Lord, it becomes confused about what to love, what to fear, and where to turn. Among the surahs of the Quran, Al-Ikhlas brings together immense knowledge of Allah in four short ayahs. People learn who it is they worship, call upon, and rely on. In light of this knowledge, they reconsider how they relate to their fellow creatures, to the means they use, and to themselves.

This surah is four ayahs long, yet it is almost constantly present in a Muslim’s worship. Muslims start the day with it and Al-Kafirun in the sunnah prayer of Fajr, recite both in the sunnah prayer after Maghrib, recite Al-Ikhlas in Witr, and read it at bedtime with the two surahs of refuge. The recitation of Al-Kafirun and Al-Ikhlas in the sunnah of Fajr is established [Muslim 726], and their recitation after Maghrib is reported [At-Tirmidhi 431]. Recitation of Al-Ikhlas in Witr is established [Ibn Majah 1172]. It is established that, when the Prophet ﷺ went to his bed, he recited Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq, and An-Nas, blew into his cupped hands, and wiped as much of his body as he could three times [Al-Bukhari 5017]. Since the believer returns to these words many times by day and night, the point goes beyond memorizing them or becoming so familiar with their sound that the heart no longer attends to them. The aim of repeating them is to renew what the believer knows about their Lord’s attributes and to move from knowing them to loving and revering Him and recognizing their need for Him.

Repeating the surah at the beginning and end of the day reminds one that Allah’s oneness is constant through all circumstances. A person may spend the night in hardship and rise to relief, or begin a day with plenty and then encounter difficulty. Their Lord, whom they turn to, does not change in His attributes when their circumstances change. Repeated recitation brings the heart back to the same truth each time, so certainty does not dissolve amid dealings with people and attachments to them. The value of repetition lies in the knowledge, love, and action it renews as the tongue moves.

A remarkable report about this surah shows the virtue of loving it. The Prophet ﷺ sent a man in command of a detachment. When he led his companions in prayer, he finished his recitation with ‘Say: “He is Allah, the One[1];’ [112:1]. Asked why he always did so, he answered in these words: “because it mentions the qualities of the Beneficent and I love to recite it (in my prayer).” The Prophet ﷺ said, “Tell him that Allah loves him.” [Al-Bukhari 7375]. Another report concerns a man of the Ansar who led the people of the Quba Mosque in prayer. He started each rakʿah with Al-Ikhlas before reciting another surah. His companions questioned this and asked him to recite Al-Ikhlas alone or to recite a different surah. He insisted on keeping it. They regarded him as one of the best among them and did not want another imam. When the Prophet ﷺ heard about it and asked why he always recited it, the man said, “Indeed I love it.” The Prophet ﷺ said, “Your love for it shall have you admitted into Paradise.” [At-Tirmidhi 2901].

The two accounts show an important difference between reciting the surah by habit and loving what it makes known of Allah’s attributes. The leader of the detachment finished with it, and the imam at Quba began his recitation with it. They shared a reason: it describes the Most Merciful, and they loved that description. The fruit of this love was that the Prophet ﷺ gave one of them glad tidings of Allah’s love and the other glad tidings of Paradise. For someone who knows what the surah contains and loves their Lord on that account, reciting it is more than a habit of the voice.

It is established that Al-Ikhlas is equal to a third of the Quran. The Hadith says, “By Him in Whose Hand my life is, it is equal to one-third of the Qur'an.” [Al-Bukhari 7374]. Two prominent explanations have been given for this comparison. One is that its reward is equal to the reward of reciting a third of the Quran. The other is that its subject encompasses one of the great foundations of the Quran. The Quran contains rulings, accounts, promises and warnings, and beliefs. This surah is devoted entirely to declaring Allah’s oneness and attributes. Its excellence leaves the rest of the Quran and its rulings in place and draws attention to the honor of what these four words contain. Whoever considers the surah finds that Al-Aḥad and Aṣ-Ṣamad occur as names of Allah only here, despite the surah’s brevity and its frequent recitation. These two names unite Allah’s unique perfection and creation’s need of Him. What the tongue memorizes of His names and attributes should lead the heart to love, supplication, and reliance. The surah then moves from Allah’s oneness and self-sufficiency to denying that He has a child, a parent, or an equal. Knowledge of Allah is thereby completed with the recognition that He is far above need or resemblance.

Al-Ikhlas is paired with Al-Kafirun in acts of worship, so much so that they have been called the two surahs of sincerity. Al-Kafirun shows what the servant does in affirming Allah’s oneness, disavowing the worship of any other and worshipping Him with sincerity. Al-Ikhlas makes their Lord known to them as the One who has no partner or peer. The surahs are connected in meaning. First comes knowing whom one worships, then giving expression to that knowledge in one’s worship and choices. Al-Kafirun makes the distinction in worship clear, “I do not worship what you worship,” [Al-Kāfirūn 109:2]. Al-Ikhlas describes the One who is rightly worshipped. It is inconsistent to disavow associating partners with Allah aloud and then let one’s heart become captive to fear of created beings or to an attachment befitting the Creator alone. Knowledge is inseparable from conduct. This is the belief with which people receive revelation and by which they then live whether pleased or angry, afraid or secure, in plenty or in need.

Frequent recitation should therefore be an opportunity for more reflection, going beyond saying the words. When someone loves another person for their good qualities, that love is based on knowing those qualities and their effects rather than on the letters of the person’s name. How much more does this apply to loving Allah, to whom belongs the highest description and perfection that no one shares?
